utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. D'Amato.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would like to thank the Prosecution for the session we had last night which was in line with the Court's wishes to allow us a chance to go over the shorthand notes of the witness's interviews with Dr. Kovacevic and Mr. Stakic in 1996. We would like to make the following notation for the record. We all know, the Tribunal knows, that our client is on trial for his life, and that the statements of the witnesses relating to conversations that he had with the accused are of significant importance to the defence of our client. Rule 68 is couched in a way that is extremely broad, and just to call your attention to the relevant language: "Evidence known to the Prosecutor which in any way tends to suggest the innocence or mitigate the guilt of the accused or may affect the credibility of Prosecution evidence," must be disclosed as soon as practicable. And we would like to report that our session last night was extremely productive. Comparing yesterday's testimony of this witness to the notes last night, my colleague, Mr. Ostojic will be presenting to you word changes, embellishments and selective retentions by the witness, which after all is only natural since he's not using any notes at this trial, that change the tone and the tenor of the charges and the words that he put in our client's mouth. In addition, the Prosecutor had presented to us, at the beginning of the trial, along with the indictment, a typed translation of the full notes of the witness, and we appreciated that, but there are changes in that too. There are inconsistencies that my colleague will point out between those typed versions and the notes that we read last night. In light of this, I would like to ask this Tribunal that we need some additional material that the Prosecution has been reluctant to give us. I think I can state the totality of it in a few short sentences, so you'll know exactly where we stand with this. We don't want any private matters that are in the witness's journal, we don't want any irrelevant matters, but we do want all matters that are relevant to any aspect of the testimony that Mr. Vulliamy testified in chief. Including, but not limited to, in 1992, we want all notes relating to the journey to both camps, all notes relating to the journey from both camps, and, of course, all notes taken at any time within both camps. We also, in 1992, want all notes relating to the meeting at which Dr. Kovacevic was present in Prijedor. With respect to 1996, we want, including but not limited to, all relevant materials relating to the interviews and teas with Professor Koljevic and the interviews with Mr. Milutinovic, Major Milutinovic, and any other relevant materials that touched on any aspect of Mr. Vulliamy's testimony that he gave in chief, and that would be the extent of it, but we need those, and we need those in a timely fashion, in order to be able to confront the witness with any discrepancies between those notes and his testimony in chief. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Last night, as counsel indicated, going well beyond, in fact, what the Trial Chamber directed, which was simply production of the copies of the notes, understanding the Defence might be concerned about the issue of surprise, we offered, if Mr. Vulliamy was willing to give them an informal reading, have him read the notes, so that they could make notes and decide what they wanted to do. During the course of that, we also provided not only the notes which you ordered to be produced, which were the '96 notes, but also the notes from the '92 meeting which he had. We also brought, beyond what you ordered, the actual books to that meeting, as opposed to simply bringing them to court as you directed so that they could look at the pages. What then followed, however, went beyond the pale of what was envisioned, by the end of which I simply offered that the -- as counsel had referred to them, the translations that were available are, in fact, not the translations, they are the typewritten notes which Mr. Vulliamy himself made the night following the interviews, and I offered those as the most complete record since Mr. Vulliamy himself can't even read all of his notes anymore. Those, as counsel has indicated, notes referring to the accused, the complete transcript as prepared by Mr. Vulliamy immediately after the event, were provided as part of the supporting material. They have been translated into Serbo-Croatian for the accused, as all the supporting material has been from the original indictment, so they've been aware of this since they were provided the supporting materials shortly after the time of his arrest, the complete interview, which was available for them to cross-examine on. There is, however, in that notebook, in particular for example, with the pages following on his visits to the camp, the notes of many people to whom he spoke, both victims, witnesses, and, in fact, guards. There is information contained in that book which is entirely private. As the Trial Chamber noted yesterday, this book is a private matter for the witness. It was not intended to be a record to be used for production at a trial, nor is it in most jurisdictions envisioned to be such, nor is it discloseable, except in very extreme circumstances. If the Court feels compelled in any way to grant any part of the Defence request, what we would then request is there would be, because of the sensitive nature of any material in there, an in camera review by the Trial Chamber for them to determine if there is any material that should be disclosed in those subsequent pages, at which point if there is information, that could be lifted out and turned over. However, with respect to the interviews which are the issue in question here, as we noted yesterday on the record, we believe that the most appropriate way to proceed was to have them read strictly into the record right off the top, and in hindsight it was a mistake to offer the informal reading because of the way things transpired. So we would request that if there is going to be any kind of consideration of a further review of the notebooks, it be done in camera. If we're going to deal with the notes as produced already, we have copies of both the notes and those typed transcripts which Mr. Vulliamy himself prepared immediately after the event, which we'll make available to the Trial Chamber for production into the record as we suggested yesterday at the close. But we would strongly object to any further intrusion into those books by Defence counsel, which is what was attempted last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the best evidence of what occurred would be the record which the witness made at the time. It leads, of course, to difficulties as to how we are to get at that record fairly to all sides and respecting the privacy of those records. It seems that no difficulty occurs about the 1996 interview. There is a typed record. If there are inconsistencies with the notes, then we could have the typed record, the inconsistencies could be pointed out, and the typed record could be corrected, and that way we will have a record of that conversation. So that, it seems, does not present any difficulties. Greater difficulties are presented by the 1992 notes, and clearly there may be matters in those notes which are of significance. There may be matters which are relevant to the Defence which would not appear to be significant to anybody else, only those who knew what the defence was would know the relevance of those matters. So clearly, to the extent that we think that the relevant notes from 1992 should be disclosed, we will accede to the Defence application. The question then remains as to how we are to proceed in order to balance what is relevant and significant with regard to what is irrelevant and private, and we think the only way to try and deal with that is to have a hearing in camera at which the witness will be asked about the notes, and it would seem that this is probably the most convenient time to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will go into Chambers. Is the notebook available?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Your Honour, did I understand you to say that in 1996, you are not going to give us the Milutinovic and the Professor's notes relating to that same -- because that was part of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that's a matter we can consider in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Okay, good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's deal, first of all, with the 1992 notes. (Closed session).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: e

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: (Open session).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I proceed with my cross-examination? Thank you. Good afternoon, Mr. Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, we covered some areas yesterday involving specifically notes that you may or may not have taken and notes that you shared with us actually a little bit yesterday and today. What I would like to know is to have your thoughts on whether or not the notes are more reliable historian, if you will, of the events that you took or your recollection? Which would be more trustworthy, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The notes as read earlier. They are contemporaneous notes, selections from -- taken at the time, a long conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't mean to imply anything, but just as a general concept, would you agree with me that the notes that you recorded and/or took down and having any conversations, regardless of whether it was with Dr. Kovacevic or others, that notes that you recorded are more trustworthy than a recollection that a person would have a year or two or four years later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that the notes were trustworthy as an account of what was said and written down. As you know, questions are omitted. I trust both my recollection and the notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's fair. We're going to introduce an exhibit later on, but I just want to get some background on this exhibit since we're talking about notes and I just want to follow up on that theme just briefly. I have and counsel for the Prosecution has tendered to us a witness statement that apparently you had given to the Office of the Prosecutor; correct? I mean, do you recollect giving such a statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure which witness statement this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, that might be my point, actually. How many witness statements did you give to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I gave a statement in two other trials and I've discussed -- I gave a statement in this case, I think, but I'm not sure which one you're referring to, so I can't really answer your question. Sorry, I mean I will if I know what statement is being asked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Happily.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I'll try to be more precise because I don't know which statements are out there that you made. I'm hoping that you, as a historian recollecting those things, can help me during my inquiry here. I know you gave statements in two trials, but I'm saying independent of your trial testimony, I have a witness statement that's approximately 15 pages long that was given to us from the Prosecutor's Office. It doesn't relate to any specific case and we'll talk about that once you've had a chance to review it. Is it your testimony that you gave a statement involving Dr. Kovacevic's case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may for a moment address this with the Tribunal and Presiding Judge? Your Honour, we have one statement that was tendered to us that -- and I'm not certain because there's absolutely no caption as to which case it may or may not be. It seems to me that we were told by the Prosecutor's Office, upon endorsing a receipt that this witness statement relates to another matter, not the Dr. Kovacevic matter, so if there are more than a couple statements, which we suspect there may be, based on his testimony here, and we do just want to cover it thoroughly, we need that statement as well, and I apologise if I should have brought this up earlier. I couldn't anticipate his questions on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That statement was taken by another trial team for a different matter, and that will be readily apparent from the content and the names of the people who took the statement. There was no statement taken from this witness either for Tadic or for this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So as far as the Office of the Prosecutor is concerned, that is the only statement, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Vulliamy, hearing that, would you agree with me that your recollection that you maybe gave a statement to the Prosecutor's Office in the Kovacevic case isn't true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have been interviewed by the Prosecutor's Office. What is or isn't called a statement, I don't know, but I have been interviewed by them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The statement that we're going to talk about that the Prosecutor mentioned -- and I say this respectfully -- that may or may not relate to this case, do you remember reading a 15-page document, initialling every page and ultimately signing the last page of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember doing that in another case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And when about did you do that; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me help you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pardon me, just to finish my answer, it's difficult to know without knowing which document you're referring to. I've been interviewed by the Prosecution here on a number of occasions, and I don't know which is this, and I recall signing a statement but I don't know which one this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I recognise that. That's why I was just merely trying to help you out. In fact, the statement I have, and I'm sure we can have a stipulation on that, is a statement signed by you March 28, 1997, approximately a year and a few months ago. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if that's what I've signed, then that's what you've got.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How many times did you visit with the Prosecutor's Office in connection with Dr. Kovacevic's case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In connection with Dr. Kovacevic's case, I believe only once, and that's when I was over here helping the Prosecution on another trial, called by the Prosecution on another trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Was that other trial the Tadic trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who met with you from the Prosecutor's Office in connection with Dr. Kovacevic's case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not officially, I believe, no. I think Ms. Hollis, I might have met her, you know, in the corridor, but Mr. Keegan in all formal transactions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, sir, when was that meeting with Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't exactly remember. It would have been sometime last year, I imagine, possibly earlier this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We discussed briefly at one point a typewritten statement of approximately six pages regarding notes that purport to be made by you -- and I again say that respectfully -- made by you in connection with a conversation that you had with Dr. Kovacevic in 1996. Do you know what I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm pretty sure I know you're referring to notes of the conversation I typed up the following day, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When did you give these notes that you typed up the following day after your conversation with Dr. Kovacevic to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometime last year, I think, possibly the year before. I can't remember. I think sometime last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you mail it to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you give it to him personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How was the mode of transportation of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I recall, it was on a computer disk.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you give them the disk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I sent it by courier.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you still have that disk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't. They have it, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know for sure whether or not they have this disk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do I know for sure whether they've got the disk? No, I don't. I haven't seen it since.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know if in the last few days you have had a chance to ascertain it back or take possession of it, that's why I ask. So you don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know because, no, I haven't ascertained to take it back and I haven't taken it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Forgive me for asking: Can you be a little more precise as to the time you sent the disk to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would have been sometime after I made the notes, a matter of months, but I honestly can't remember exactly when it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So is it fair to say it was a couple of months after your conversation with Dr. Kovacevic in February of 1996; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it would have been during the Tadic trial but, to the best of my recollection, after I testified in the Tadic trial, but I can't be exact, I'm afraid. I could consult my diary if I have any record of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did the courier package that contained the disk that you sent to the Prosecutor's Office, did it contain an introductory letter by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, most certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who has that introductory letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, as you sit here, a year or so ago, what that introductory letter said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't expect you to. But I don't know, some people have a much better memory.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember what I would have written in the introductory letter, but I'm sure there would have been some explanation what the disk was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How long, if you recall, was this letter to the Prosecutor's Office that accompanied the disk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember. I expect a side or something. I honestly can't remember how long the letter was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you correspond with the Prosecutor's Office in writing on any other occasions other than this one occasion that we're discussing now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What? Over the years, you mean? Yes. I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like for you to break that down for me, but I'd specifically like for you, sir, if you can, to highlight when it involved Dr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't recall written correspondence, but certainly Dr. Kovacevic was part of the preparations for my testimony in the Tadic trial, the meeting in Prijedor was mentioned. I was obliged, during that trial, to talk about the meeting, the notes of which I read this morning, to talk about the camps. My job in that trial was to establish what I think is called widespread or systematic pattern, and I would, by then, have talked about Dr. Kovacevic and my interview with him in 1996 because I can remember testifying about the conversation when I was testifying in the trial of Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Written correspondence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, I -- just so the record is clear, I would like to make a formal request to the Prosecutor, if permitted, to obtain that disk and that cover letter or any other corresponding letters between them and Mr. Vulliamy, specifically in connection with Dr. Kovacevic. Certainly, although interesting, it's not relevant on other matters and we're not asking for that at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, you can make the request. No doubt it's been noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vulliamy, you interestingly just said that your job was, and you were responsible for, certain things in the Tadic trial. What do you mean when you say it was your job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was called as what was described to me as being an expert witness and I was asked questions which -- many of which didn't seem relevant to this particular case or to this particular Defendant, but I understood later that the purpose of this was to establish a widespread or systematic pattern which was necessary for the bringing of charges in a court of this kind rather than a normal criminal court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why did you think at that time that those things the Prosecutor was asking you didn't seem relevant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was talking about places, some of which have been admitted in this trial, some of which haven't -- look, I'm not a lawyer. My understanding of the difference between this Court and an ordinary court in a country is that of which people are accused here has to be part of a pattern, and I think you'd better ask them. The Prosecution at the time in that case was interested in the fact that I had been in Bosnia for, on and off, mostly on, between 1991 and 1996 and that I had a widespread view of what was going on and did I think that something systematic was happening? That's what they were asking me and they were asking me about the full spectrum.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm just pausing for the interpreter because yesterday I was admonished about it, so I appreciate you waiting for my next question. Sir, did the Prosecutors tell you that, in fact, they needed certain elements within their case, regardless whose case it is, including Dr. Kovacevic's, therefore they were asking and inquiring and shaping your views of the war in order to fit certain elements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not knowing they needed this systematic, as you called it, plan, were they asking you questions or did they initially tell you that "We need to establish a systematic plan. Can you give us the facts which may or may not support that?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were asking questions. I knew more about the war than they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who is the "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The prosecuting lawyer in that case was Michael Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so that we're clear which case we're talking about. Was that the Tadic trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic. I also was asked to give similar evidence in a different trial, that of Mr. Blaskic, and was called to do so and did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Again, I'm trying to get a time frame so that we don't cover a period that's outside the scope of the Tribunal's ruling and also to try to limit it to keep it in perspective for you. The disk and the Tadic conversation that you had with Mr. Keegan regarding establishing yourself as a "expert," which came first? Did you deliver the disk to the Prosecutor's Office or did you first met with Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met with Mr. Keegan for the first time before I sent him the disk, yes, definitely. I first met Mr. Keegan long before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: A couple more questions just on the disk, and I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You had this disk, and is it your testimony that you typed into your computer immediately after your visit with Dr. Kovacevic in 1996, based on your notes, the conversations that you had with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The typewritten notes you're talking about were written the following day in Zagreb as an aide-memoire -- if anyone's calling them transcripts, then I don't accept that, they were an aide-memoire to myself in order to organise the material thematically in preparation to writing an article, which is my prime responsibility, and it was a question of organising the material that I had and -- in a way that I could make sense of it for a reader, who I was thinking about at the time, not a court of law, and also there was the fact that my colleague had been with me at the same meeting, and we were comparing recollections of the meeting and organising the material. As regards the disk, that was sent to The Hague sometime afterwards, between then and when I testified, and I will endeavour to find an exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I would appreciate that, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I'll try to find if there's any receipt of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say for purposes of a time line that we can use -- what month in 1996? I said February and you didn't correct me, and that's fair, but I think yesterday your testimony was you met with Dr. Kovacevic in mid 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I don't want to be unfair to you, so whatever your recollection is, I would just like to be clear on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: February 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you at any time, after inputting the data from your conversation with Dr. Kovacevic in February 1996, download or print the information from your disk prior to sharing it with the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember whether I downloaded or whether I just used it on an alternative screen on the computer when I was writing. Yes, I think I would have probably had it printed up or printed it out, but I can't remember. I wouldn't have had it printed in Zagreb where I was that day because there was no means to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you share with us when, if at all, did you print it out and where is that printed statement or notes, those printed notes? When did you do it and where are they today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it was printed up in Zagreb, it would have been at a friend's house. If it was printed up in London, it would have been back at the office. I don't remember. But it would have been at either of those, and I don't know where the original of that is today.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At any time, sir, did you endeavour to find that original?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What I'd like to know is, if you shared those notes with anyone other than the Office of the Prosecutor at any time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to my immediate recollection, no, I don't think I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you were inputting this information in a computer. How long has it been prior to 1996 that you started using a computer to input your notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How long -- any notes?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Any notes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I first started work on the newspaper, which was in 1986, the system was computerised about a year afterwards, so it would be 1987.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: During your time in former Yugoslavia, in Croatia, and you took us through a little journey which we'll visit again through Bosnia and Herzegovina, did you have a computer with you during that period, '91 through '92?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in Bosnia much, no. If people used computers, we used them from the coastal hotels in Croatia. When we were in Bosnia, there was no electricity, so it wasn't much use having a computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So you didn't have a computer with you during your journey through Bosnia, or did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which journey?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The one through -- from January through August of 1992, that period in particular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: August 1992. I wasn't there in January through -- but in 1992, no, I didn't have a computer with me, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you have a computer during your journey through different parts of Croatia and/or Bosnia from August -- or mid August 1992 through what? How long were you there? December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there, I mean, on and off, a lot longer than that. No, I didn't have a computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just want to clarify it because you said that you did start bringing a computer in '88, and I just want to know if, when you had a computer and you were in Zagreb for different periods of time, because I think your testimony was that after your visit in Trnopolje and at Omarska, you went for a day or two to rest in Zagreb, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, after going to Omarska and Trnopolje, we went to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you have a computer that you used in Belgrade during that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you input in that computer that which you witnessed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Where is that computer and those notes today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That computer is an old thing called a Tandy with a very small letterbox-like screen. They were jettisoned by my paper a long time ago. I don't know where that machine is. In the rubbish, I should think.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you still maintain any of the disks from your journey in 1992 specifically August of ‘92, in July of ‘92?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no way of putting a disk into that type of equipment, so no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you have any other notes or any other records, either in your home, your office, or a colleague or friend's home, involving what you had seen in your journeys through Bosnia in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The notes are here. I read them to you. I may have written stuff in personal diaries, but that's private, and I don't even know where they are now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we did just become familiar with those notes. I'm talking about any other notes, as you sit here, do you recall that you had which involve your journey through Bosnia and Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote a book which was written during the summer of 1993 and completed shortly after, published early the next year, and there are a lot of source materials for that, newspaper cuttings, notes that I took when talking to colleagues, notes from other newspaper cuttings, notes from books, and some of that pertains to 1992, if that's what you mean, but this is research from what I would call secondary sources, not from my own visit. They are those which I have already tendered to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not concerned with the secondary sources at this time. I just want to make sure that I've covered all the notes that you have and all the notes that you may have in connection with Dr. Kovacevic. Is it a fair statement that all the notes you have regarding Dr. Kovacevic and the time that you were in Prijedor are included within those two volumes or books, as we'll call them, that are before you today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And my personal diaries, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm going to have to ask you, and I apologise, how extensive are your notes in your personal diaries in connection with Dr. Kovacevic's case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the diaries -- I keep -- kept a diary which was a small page per day, and certainly there were personal recollections of those visits to Omarska and Trnopolje. I actually can't remember whether Dr. Kovacevic is mentioned by name in those. I shouldn't think so. But certainly the meeting and the impressions of the day as read out from this book would be mentioned in my personal diary, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It seems clear, but I just want to make sure I have a straight answer to a hopefully straight question, and that is: Did you keep a contemporaneous diary during your visit through the Prijedor area in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The diary I would have written when we got back to Belgrade. I didn't have the -- my personal diary with me when we were wandering around Prijedor and Banja Luka, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, sir, you still maintain that diary from those years; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't. I imagine it's in storage somewhere. I don't have it available. Not now anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Where is it in storage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could be either in London or in a place called Gaithersburg, Maryland.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If possible, would there be any way to retrieve that diary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll have a look for it if I've still got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to move onto another section. I'm done with the notes. Let me ask this last question: Have we completed or exhausted your recollection of any notes, records, CDs, I mean compact disks or any similar type of information in connection with your recordings of any visits you had between Dr. Kovacevic in 1992 and 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we have, yes. 1996, I was no longer keeping a page-a-day diary. There may be some notes from a conversation with my colleague with whom I went to see Dr. Kovacevic when I was compiling my aide-memoire, but I no longer have those.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Does your colleague have them, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well -- no, I took the notes talking to him on the phone so, no, because he never had them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I want to focus a couple of questions at this point regarding the first meeting that you had at the municipal building in 1992 and your discussions briefly about that yesterday. I'll go back into it in a little more detail, so my questions are just to kind of get an understanding of exactly the time period, who's present, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In 1992, specifically July 1992, did you have an interpreter to assist you with the translation between various parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: August 1992 we met Dr. Kovacevic. Do you mean July or August?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I know you went through Belgrade on July 28th, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- and I'm really concerned if you -- strike that. I'm really curious to know if you had an interpreter even through that travel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were two interpreters, both employed by ITN, and one -- I don't know their second names, I'm afraid, one you can see in the television shots quite a lot, the gentleman in the jeans with glasses, and there was a lady with the second crew, whose name I never knew, and she is in the shot a couple of times. I could identify her, if you want. And she's wearing a white top. But they were doing translating, yes. Some of the translations were also done by Mrs. Balaban of the Prijedor council, as you can see on the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At this point, Mr. Vulliamy, I'm only concerned with the interpreters that were retained by you or on your behalf, so -- and I'm just trying to keep it narrow so we can move along and get to some other points. Other than these two -- strike that. With respect to your visit from July 1992 through -- was it August 7th that you left Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I left Prijedor on the evening of August the 5th for Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just so we have a proper time frame, when did you arrive there? August 2nd?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there for my birthday, so I think it would have been July 30th, 31st, more likely 30th. That's a date I can easily get for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's what I thought I read somewhere, but you confused me a little when I asked you the question of whether you were in Prijedor in July, you forced me to think it was in August, but, in fact, you were there in July 30th or 31st, right around that period.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we were in Belgrade July 30th, 31st. We left for Prijedor from Pale on -- I can give you the date if you give me a moment. We left -- we went into the camps on August the 5th, so we would have left Banja Luka for Prijedor on the morning of August the 5th and Pale for Banja Luka on the day before that, which would have been August the 4th. Therefore leaving Belgrade for Pale on August the 3rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So in connection with your visit in 1992 and Dr. Kovacevic, how many days were you specifically in that Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that would have been August 5th; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: August the 5th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, is it fair to say that on August 5th, 1992, one or both of the interpreters accompanied you throughout your -- I don't want to call it a mission, but let's call it that. Throughout your mission in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't call it a mission. Throughout that day's work on August the 5th, 1992, there were two interpreters employed by ITN whom I was also using and there was also Mrs. Balaban in Omarska. At Trnopolje, there were two prisoners who spoke good English, whose names I'm not going to provide, if that's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we're not asking. Thank you. What I want to know is whether or not the interpreters accompanied you through your entire period of August 5th from Prijedor to Omarska and then through Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, apart from a short period when I toured the Trnopolje camp just by myself with a prisoner who spoke English and who took me round the back of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so I can get a little idea of where you were when you went in the back there. I think you mentioned that you essentially had free access through that camp, Trnopolje; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Relatively, yes. The bit that we first arrived at was a compound into which we could not go, but further behind that was an area into which we could -- well, apparently because I did -- whether it was permissible or not, I don't know -- but into which I was able to go with this prisoner, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With this person that you went to visit around the camp, what area were you going to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was an area around a school, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know or if you can recall whether or not you had an occasion to meet a gentleman that we saw on the video who I think was referred to as a doctor, a Muslim doctor, who gave you an interview, and I'm not sure what his designation was but I think he's referred to as the Muslim doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was there when he was being interviewed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I know you were there when he was being interviewed and you shared that with us yesterday in some detail. That was when he was in with Penny Marshall and you stated --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the crew was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You stated you were behind her.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was on the -- yeah, on the edge of a group of people listening, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: My question really is -- we're now trying to focus on this period that you went around by the school yard with this person who was able to interpret for you who was not the official, if you will, or your two interpreters that you identified earlier. Did you visit with this doctor while this interpreter was accompanying you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The conversation with the doctor was being translated by one of the ITN translators.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How many conversations did you have with this doctor on August 5th, 1992, at the Trnopolje area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't call the time when I was there while they were filming him a conversation because I didn't say anything. I was just listening and watching, and I briefly spoke to him for about two minutes, I think about 15 minutes later.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We heard your testimony about what the tape said and what you recalled about it and what you felt his features, and I think you gave us an interesting account of what you felt he was thinking at the time, and if you recall -- I'm just trying to jog your memory to your testimony -- you will recall you mentioned that although not seen on the video, there is a guard or a military person nearby; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I recall, there were quite a few, yeah. Then and at the other town.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What I didn't get yesterday in your testimony was the second -- or this first conversation that you had with this doctor, do you recall that, as you sit here, how long that conversation was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conversation he has with the camera, you mean? I didn't actually talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the translator. We heard the conversation that was taped and we heard your testimony about the conversation that was taped. Was there a conversation between you and this medical doctor that was off the record that we haven't heard about yet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure I follow that. The witness has said that he had a -- as I understand it -- he was present during the interview by the ITN reporter, as part of a group, and subsequently spoke to the doctor himself about a quarter of an hour later. Is that right, Mr. Vulliamy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is the way I understood it. Whether that was on or off the record, I'm not sure what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It doesn't. And frankly I wanted to go to this conversation and I'm struggling for one reason or another with this witness to get to that conversation. My intent is for him to share that particular conversation with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. It wasn't very successful because, by then, the ITN interpreters had gone and the prisoner was with me, and he was being called away. But what I was trying to ascertain was whether the Red Cross had come into this place. We talked about the Red Cross, the International Red Cross, in Omarska, and I wanted to know whether he was getting any help from the International Red Cross in this place, Trnopolje, and, as I recall, he said, no, we only get help from the Serbian Red Cross, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So this doctor, the same one we saw the video of, he told you during this conversation that the Serbian Red Cross was providing medicines and supplies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How long was that conversation between you and the doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thirty seconds? A minute?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't want to put a time limit but, I mean, very short, yes, something of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is there anything else that the doctor told you about in that conversation that you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He talked about shortages of various drugs that he wanted to have in order to do his job properly. That was about the sum total of the conversation, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Nothing else; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that I recall now, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention, if I may, because I am still a bit uncomfortable with our conversations earlier, to specifically his notes in connection with the visit at Trnopolje and the contents of a conversation he had with the medical doctor that he shared with us today, so I'm trying not to divulge what it is, but I'd like to direct his attention because I think it's a bit more broader than the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the written note, the contemporaneous note.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which the witness has got -- Mr. Vulliamy, if you can find the relevant part --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There will be a note of that conversation in here, so I can read it to you, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I apologise. You have the volume in front of you? Can you turn to the section in connection with Trnopolje in which you took contemporaneous notes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Trnopolje. I'm trying to find the bit with the doctor. That's what you want me to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At this time I'm only interested in the bit with the doctor and then we're going to move on. Hopefully with the permission of the Court we're going to come back to that in a different manner. But right now we're only focusing on your recollection and we've exhausted it and now the contents of the conversation that you had with the medical doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you want me to find that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. This will be it here. It's at the bottom of the page. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just out of curiosity, how long is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's five lines and two words.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With the permission of the Court, may he read that in, here today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. There's no reason why the witness shouldn't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at all: Red Cro in this area we have only help from the Serbian, we have no adequate antibiotics, insulin, plasma, vaccinations, first class medicines. In this area some children are dying because anti-bio/insulin.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is there anything else in connection with the note that you have there with the doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that I can see unless it goes over the page. No. Then I talked to another doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Another what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Another doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is this other doctor a different doctor than the doctor that was on the video screen that we saw yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How long is that entry with that doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second doctor?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He's from the Yugoslav Red Cross, this second doctor, and it's one, two, three ... eight lines with the word "twenty babies" underneath, and I don't know what that is, and a bottom line. So nine lines all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did the Yugoslav Red Cross doctor ever tell you how long he had been at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever ask him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall asking him, no. My question to him was for -- was whether he had visited Omarska and for his judgement on the medical conditions there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll get back to the transcript with the permission of the Court or to the notes with the permission of the Court at a later time. I just wanted to clarify that one point, thank you. If I may proceed on another area? Sir, generally, I'd like to get an outline of the time parameters in which you were through Croatia and Bosnia, Belgrade, etc. I have my notes, and correct me if I'm wrong, that from June 1991 through December 1991, you were in the Croatian part of former Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most but not all of the time. We were covering the war in shifts, and we were coming and going. That is the right time frame that I was there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: From January 1992 through July 1992, where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was working elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Italy, I was in Croatia once, and in England.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, were you ever in Sarajevo in July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm familiar with your journey in connection with Dr. Kovacevic's statements and then your departure to come to Belgrade and through Belgrade, then I understand it to be into Prijedor on August 5th and then back out, et cetera. That I thought occurred, your actual arrival in Belgrade was July 28th, 199 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Something like that, yes. I can get that date for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Were you in Sarajevo prior to July 28th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So it would have been sometime between July 28th through July 31st, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were with Mr. Karadzic's guards for a while, and on the -- all around Sarajevo and in a place called Grbavica and in Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How long were you there? How many days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A day -- well, the best part of an afternoon and early evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We know from your testimony that you left Prijedor area on or about August 5th, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Take me through August 6th, 1992, through mid August 1992, just generally tell me where you were? If it was multiple places, excuse me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No no, it's OK. Right, I'm trying to do this from memory. The story was published -- the story about the camps was published on August the 7th, 1992, the -- I left Belgrade -- it was (inaudible) on the 7th, I left Belgrade I think on the 8th or the 9th, I'm not quite sure, and drove through Hungary to get to the Croatian side to take up the challenge to inspect camps on that side, I went to Zagreb, the camps that I wanted to look at were down in the Herzegovina area, so I went down there. I was in Split, Capljina, around that area, back up to Zagreb. Some days later, I went to Mostar. I was in Herzegovina for quite a long time around that time. I went up to Zagreb, I went to -- then I went on that long road with the refugees with the deportees over into Travnik, I was in Travnik --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt. That's the area and it's this voyage that you took that I was particularly curious about, and that's why I asked the question. Can you give me a time frame of when all this occurred? I recognise that we're somewhere after August 9th, 1992, but if we can just be precise, with the Court's permission, how long it took for you to go through Croatia and the various places up until the point you came to this convoy as you described it yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let's see, I leave Belgrade, the drive from Belgrade to Zagreb would have been the best part of the day, Zagreb to the coast, there is a flight down to Split to pick up a car, visit to the people who were running the camp, the Croatian camp, that was in a place called Ljubuski in Herzegovina, that's a day and a bit, I suppose we must be -- I'm guessing here, but I think we're sometime around the 10th or the 12th of August. Mostar around that time, Ljubuski around that time, Capljina around that time, went in the camp, went back to Split, got a plane to Zagreb, and this is all days and half-days, and I would have got a plane back to Zagreb sometime around the 15th, I think, because on the -- I'd like to check this with the published papers, if I may? -- but I think our journey over the mountains with the deportees was the 17th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mid August; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mid -- yeah, mid August.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like, if I may, with the Court's permission, read -- because we do not have at this time photocopies of the statement that the Prosecutor provided us. I believe it's familiar to him -- them, I should say, and with the Court's permission, I'd like to read it, and it's the statement of Mr. Vulliamy in connection with this period that we're talking about, in mid August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there a copy for the witness who should have one? There isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: We certainly didn't bring it into the courtroom, Your Honour. We didn't know he was going to be questioned on his statement, so I'm afraid I don't have one available right here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And you don't have one, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I don't. I can tender, with the Court's permission, this one. I did take some notes in connection with it. I don't want to be fair -- I think my words, I put them around quotes, should specifically reflect this, that I wrote down, but I again I apologise, I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, put the passage to the witness, and if need be, you must hand the document to him to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we may mark it as Defence Exhibit 4, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Five, thank you. Sir -- if I may proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, you have Defence Exhibit number 5 in front of you; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Me?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just so we have the record clear, can you tell us, with respect to Defendant's Exhibit number 5, what is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Witness statement, initialled by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How many pages is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fourteen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And does your signature appear on the last page of that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you've initialled each page of the document; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to that document, I just want to clarify one point. We were engaged in a bit of a discussion of what that document is and how it is, if you recall, and I'd like for you to flip to the first page of the document. Can you tell me, from reviewing the first page of the document, whether or not Dr. Kovacevic's case or name is anywhere mentioned on that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which case or if any name is mentioned on that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't see the name of the case, but I can tell you, if you want to know, it's Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like -- and I appreciate what you can tell me, but I'm focusing on the document because I want to know -- and we'll decide later who decides whether these documents belong in which case -- but I'd like to know, for the record, if you could find for me in this 15-page document any mention of any case that you've ever testified to, including Blaskic or Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You want me to read this -- say what?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't want you to read it, Mr. Vulliamy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Put it to the witness that there is no mention of any particular case. In due course, no doubt, if there is mention, it can be raised, but for the moment, you could put it in general terms rather than have the witness read the entire statement now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Truly, I didn't mean for you to read the entire statement here. I apologise for that. I'm just looking generally for the caption, but I will summarise and ask you a pointed question: Isn't it true, sir, in that document, from your brief review here, there is absolutely no mention of any case that is the supposed written statement belonging to -- that was a terrible question, I recognise that, and if the Court would like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no mention of Mr. Kovacevic. That's established. Does it really matter whether there's a mention of anybody else or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think it does, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's our position that this was a general statement made by Mr. Vulliamy in connection -- to be used in every case, and this is something the Prosecution did. They didn't put a case. Earlier his testimony was, quite candidly, that he did give a statement specifically to that case. I don't see the case mentioned. If someone can assist us like the Prosecutor to tell us that within this document this specific statement is for a particular case, not including Dr. Kovacevic. There's mention of his voyage in July of 1992 within that statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why don't we come to that? The purpose of the statement really doesn't matter, does it? As far as the witness's evidence is concerned, it's the contents rather than why the Prosecution may have taken the statement. Let's come to the journey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it helps the Court, I recall exactly for which case and by the Prosecution in which case this statement was taken, and it was that in the case of Mr. Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, I'm directing your attention to page 2 of that document, and I believe midway through that document -- forgive me for not having a copy of it before me -- you state, and I quote: "The area generally controlled by the Croatian Defence Council or HVO and the Muslims -- I apologise. The Muslim-led Bosnian government army. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who was the leader of the Bosnian -- or the Muslim-led Bosnian government army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a reference to the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic, and I would imagine the General in charge of the army at the time, who I think was called Delic who were both Muslims and leading the Bosnian government army. I say Muslim-led because not all the people in it were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, what other people were in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbs and some Croats. In fact, the deputy leader of that army was another General who was a Serb called Divjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned that he was a General, Divjak. Do you know the General's first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't. I'm afraid I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, as you sit here, how to spell his last name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: D-I-V-I-J-A-K, as I recall or maybe just D-I-V-J-A-K, something of that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you speak any different foreign languages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I speak Italian, I speak French, and I have very rusty Spanish, but I wouldn't want to bank on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you speak Serbo-Croatian or a derivative of that language, whatever people identify it with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I would not want to lay that claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, during your trip to Prijedor in July of 1992, was there an atmosphere of cooperation between the HVO and the Bosnian, or the Muslim-led Bosnian -- strike that. Sir, during your journey in July of 1992, was there an atmosphere of cooperation between the HVO and the Muslim-led Bosnian government army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I first arrived in Bosnia in July '92, do you mean, and thereafter? Yes, there was, at first.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Refresh my recollection. When you first arrived in Bosnia, would that have been July 28th or thereabouts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, July 28th, yeah. Yes, at that time the two -- the two armies were fighting together, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, did you ever use the term "atmosphere of cooperation" within that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember. I'd have to have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On page 6, if you would turn to that page -- I can't direct you to it, I apologise. My notes only suggest that it seems to be there. I don't want to approach the witness. With the Court's permission, may I have the document back? Perhaps I could find it quicker? Thank you. May I proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In the second full paragraph on page 6, do you see in the third line there, approximately, the words "atmosphere of cooperation?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what "atmosphere of cooperation" is, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it means that the two components in this cooperation seemed to be on the same side, in this case in a war. In general I think it means that people are -- have common cause or are cooperating with each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your words, sir, and I'm just trying to understand exactly what they mean. I can interpret them, and I would just like to know what you meant. That's why I ask. Thank you. You described for us, did you not, that the Muslim-led Bosnian government army consisted of, in essence, Bosnian Muslims, Serbs -- you mentioned the General -- and Croats; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning, it was -- at the beginning, that army was mostly Muslim and Muslim-led, as I've tried to explain, but did contain officers and soldiers from other ethnic groups, markedly Serbs and some Croatians. As the war proceeded, that became less the case and it became more Muslim. At the time we're talking about, your description is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So post-July and August 1992, the Bosnian government army, would it be fair to say, contained fewer and fewer Serb officers and Serbian soldiers and fewer and fewer Croatian officers and Croatian soldiers? We're talking about the period after August 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After October 1992, in particular, the Bosnian army -- the Bosnian government army would have contained very much fewer Croats because a war, a side show war, had started between, or was starting between the Bosnian government army and the Croatian HVO. The number of Serbs in the Bosnian government army decreased over a longer period of time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it also then fair to say that prior to, before July 1992, there were more and more Serbian officers and Serbian soldiers and likewise Croatian officers and Croatian soldiers who were within the Bosnian government army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before summer 1992, there were more Serbs and Croats in the Bosnian government army than there were say a year later, thereafter, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Specifically with respect to this matter in Prijedor, is there a date that we could cut off and say, "Well, August 1st, there were more or less Serbian soldiers and Serbian military within the Bosnian government army," or really it's difficult to say and all you could do for us is give us a general overlap, two, three, eight-week period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge in the Prijedor area, and as I've already told the Court, I didn't go there until August 1992, I was gleaning material from the papers and television and have since acquired my knowledge from reading and secondary sources, but to the best of my knowledge in Prijedor, it would not really be appropriate to talk about a Bosnian government army. Before the Bosnian government army got itself organised, it was called the TO or Territorial Defence, I believe, and I'm not sure whether the army was in a position to establish brigades or anything like that in Prijedor. I think it had more or less gone by then and would have called itself the TO, which was, if you like, its antecedent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On page 6 we mentioned the atmosphere of cooperation between the HVO and the Muslim-led Bosnian government army. I believe it also states -- and I can quote it: "And the atmosphere of cooperation between the HVO and the Muslims that were noticed before and which" -- can you follow me? Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm following you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you read that statement into the record for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The atmosphere -- this is about the town of Mostar. "The atmosphere of cooperation between the HVO and Muslims that we noticed before and which had led to the defeat of the Serbs in July was now completely gone."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the period of time you're talking about there, when you say the cooperation was gone, is October of 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is an observation made, I can see from my statement, on the 24th of October, 1992, referring back to that July, the July of that same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So looking at that statement, would it be fair to say that on or about October 24th, 1992, the atmosphere of cooperation between at least the HVO and the Muslim-led Bosnian government army, as you put it, "was gone."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In July, the month to which I refer, the two armies, the HVO and the Bosnian army, had fought alongside one another and pushed the Serbian forces back to an area east of the Neretva river. When I go back in October 1992, I find that the atmosphere of cooperation -- there was not an atmosphere of cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you questions generally prior to and after July-August 1992 with respect to the Bosnian government army, and you initially identified for us one Serbian General that was within that army during that period, and then in my subsequent questions I said officers, and I just want the record to be clear. I don't mean to suggest that there was more than one. But would it be fair to state that, in fact, there were officers, plural, and soldiers, plural, who were Serbians who were within the Bosnian government army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were some.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, we will be taking a break when you come to a convenient moment. Would that be a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It may be, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I proceed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, we were generally discussing on Defendant's Exhibit number 5 earlier, and we now have a copy, and I want to thank the Office of the Prosecutor for providing that to us. Sir, directing your attention to page 9 of that exhibit, let me just ask you a general question: When you talked about your journey through Travnik -- do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The journey to Travnik over the mountains, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Was that the journey that you described yesterday where you joined a convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we're talking about the same journey, yes, that's the one, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you have more than one journey to Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several journeys to Travnik. I was talking about the specific one with the convoy of people from Sanski Most when I was talking yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you join more than one convoy during your several visits to the area of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were various convoys. There was the one I was talking about from Jajce which we joined a long way along its course into Travnik, but the main convoy that I joined was that which I described yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On page 9 you discuss Jajce and Travnik on paragraphs two and three; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Generally, would that be about the time that you were discussing with us your convoys yesterday through Jajce and Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The convoys I believe we discussed yesterday were two. One was in mid August 1992 which I took -- which I accompanied all the way from just outside Prijedor over the mountains into Travnik, and this one, this late October 1992, in the second paragraph of this page, is talking about the people coming out of Jajce into Travnik later in the year which I also described yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You described somewhat compelling how many refugees were with you in this convoy. I think you mentioned that there were 15 cars, eight or so buses and you mentioned other vehicles, modes of transportation; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think it was 55.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we're talking about the mid August, indeed, 55 or so cars and a dozen or so trucks and buses, ten, twelve, trucks and buses. That's on the mid August convoy from Prijedor to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, it states here on page 9 that the convoy that you were on apparently in Jajce through Travnik, that: The result was the largest exodus of the war, approximately 40.000 refugees poured into Travnik while I was there. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What period of time are we talking about there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What this was was, and I wrote this in the paper at the time, the largest single exodus of the war, that is to say, the largest according to the figures that I could get, at least, and I think they were produced in documents yesterday from official bodies, the largest single movement of population at one time, 40.000 in the space of just over a day, some 36 hours, was the largest single movement of people in that short space of time of the war to date and the time frame we're talking about is the end of October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't see that "single" in there, the word, "the single largest exodus." But be that as it may, with respect to Jajce, on the paragraph immediately preceding that, what period of time are you talking about there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry? Jajce fell at the end of October 1992. The exodus from Jajce was, as I recall, going into -- it was the Saturday around the first day of November 1992. I don't remember whether that was the first of second or the last day of October, but that's the sort of time frame.
