utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say you made two journeys: one in August through Travnik and Jajce, and then one later in October of 1992 through Jajce and Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't get to Jajce. What I said was that in August 1992, I joined a convoy at Lamovitza and stayed with it all the way to Travnik, and the second convoy that you're talking about here was one which I accompanied only in its latter stage from a place called Karaula, which is towards Jajce, not in Jajce, back into Travnik; that is to say, we went out to meet it, joined it, and came back into town with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Does Defendant's Exhibit number 5, this 15 or so page document, at all reflect the voyage that you shared with us through Jajce, Travnik, Lamovitza in August of 1992? Is it reflected here anywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it shouldn't be here because this statement was given to the Prosecution in a case that pertained to the other war which I talked about, and that is the war between the Muslim-led -- the Muslims and the Croats, if you like, the HVO and the ABiH in Central Bosnia, so that they weren't really particularly interested in ethnic cleansing from Serbian areas, their concern was the Lasva Valley area and Herzegovina, and so if I do go into the August convoy in detail in this statement, I'm wasting their time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So is it fair to say the answer is "No"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, I haven't read it, but I shouldn't think it's here in much detail because it wouldn't have been of interest to the Prosecution in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did the Prosecution in that case also discuss with you the possibility of you becoming an "expert" witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that was my title. I'm not sure. I was called to testify on what I had seen with regard to the war between the HVO and the ABiH or Bosnian army from October 1992 onwards, a war that concluded in February 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did they also want you to establish that pattern that you discussed, that you talked about in this case, for other matters as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You talked a little bit about this pattern that the Prosecution wanted to establish, and we discussed it briefly before the break. Did they discuss this pattern that they wanted to establish also in your meeting with them in connection with the statement -- I know they're going to explain it, and I appreciate your explanation to us -- but in connection with this statement that you prepared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were asking me about the pattern of the HVO and Bosnian Croat plans with regard to Muslims in the terrain that the Croatians were interested in. What they were trying to establish, you had better ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When was the first time that Mr. Keegan or the Office of the Prosecutor sought you out to be an expert witness to establish anything in connection with the former Yugoslavia and the civil war that was going on there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, I'm not going to stop you, but you have cross-examined very extensively on this topic, and I wonder if it's going to assist us to hear more cross-examination on these matters. You've been over the statements, with respect, and you've been through the notes. Perhaps we could move on?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may just have an answer to that last question? I was wrapping up this area. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When Mr. Keegan first contacted me, I was living in Washington temporarily and the indictment had been made for the trial of Dusko Tadic, so all I -- well, I can say that it would have been before April 1995 when I went back -- came back to Europe and soon after to Bosnia. I expect it was towards the end of 1994 or perhaps the spring of 1995. I would guess the latter. Early 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Again, just so I have time frames down, end of 1994, spring or April 1995, you were first contacted by Mr. Keegan or the Office of the Prosecutor to potentially become a witness, and that would be an "expert" witness in connection with an indictment that was served or pending; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether -- when the contact was first made. It was suggested that I testify. I don't recall whether or not, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So you don't recall if it was end of '94 or early '95. My question is this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It was definitely before your meeting with Dr. Kovacevic in 1996; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Approximately a year or so before your meeting and conversation with Dr. Kovacevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I imagine so. Something like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When the Prosecution communicated with you to be a witness in the Tadic case, or whichever case it was that they sought your services for, did they tell you that they were going to reimburse you in any way for your time and expense?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a standard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're not going to suggest that, are you, that this witness is somehow influenced by money or anything of that sort?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not, and I wouldn't ask the amount, respectfully, or anything. I was just curious to know if it was at all, and that's all. So I apologise. I can withdraw the question if the court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think it's of any assistance, really.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am perfectly happy to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And my apologies, Mr. Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So did the Prosecution at all, when you visited with them in late 1994 or 1995, one year prior to your visit with Dr. Kovacevic, did they discuss with you in detail the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did Dr. Kovacevic's name come up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you whether or not they were going to try or attempting to procure evidence to determine whether or not they can indict Dr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What, if anything, did they tell you about Dr. Kovacevic during your visits on or about the period that you were first retained or asked to give testimony in connection to these matters before the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think they told me anything about him. We were talking about the camps in which Mr. Tadic was charged with having been.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did Dr. Kovacevic's name ever come up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In what capacity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the capacity of the notes that you've seen. He was there at the meeting and before we went into Omarska and was introduced as having been in charge of -- officer of the civilian authorities that were running them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You use the word "in charge." I noticed earlier yesterday and a bit the day before, an hour or so. When you say "chairman" and "in charge," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Did most of the talking at the meeting and was introduced to us by Colonel Arsic as one of the people to whom we should address ourselves if we wish to persist in our request to go to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to know, sir, if you can tell me, from early 1995, before the meeting with Dr. Kovacevic in 1996, and we've established it was sometime in February 1996, how many times did you visit with the Prosecutor's Office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once or twice. I can't remember how many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It being three years ago, what, if anything, would refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if I -- I suppose if I were to ask Mr. Keegan if he remembers how many times. I think I first came here in the winter of -- autumn-winter 1995, to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would that have been the second time you met with him, because the first time I have down here is sometime in early 1995, and I don't know if you're calling "winter" that early part of 1995 or the latter part of 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I first met Mr. Keegan in Washington, DC in the early part of 1995. If it turns out to have been the latter part of 1994, then I'm to be corrected, but I think it's the early part of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Where did you meet Mr. Keegan in Washington?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Whose office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My office.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Washington, DC

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you give me the address of the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. 1730 Rhode Island Avenue, Northwest.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Was that the office for your professional life being with The Guardian, or were you in some other capacity in Washington, DC?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the bureau of The Guardian in Washington.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How long was your meeting with Mr. Keegan in Washington in 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not very long. I think between half an hour and an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you exchange any documents with him during that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you keep notes of your meeting with Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you correspond with Mr. Keegan at any time after this initial meeting in 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think I would have -- I can't remember, actually. I don't think so, no. There might have been telephone contact prior to my first visit here. I'm sure there would have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That was the first meeting. Now, take me to any other meetings that you had with Mr. Keegan from 1995 up until February 1996 when you met with Dr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was invited to come here from London formally in the -- to the best of my recollection - if Mr. Keegan has another record, I stand corrected - but I think it was in the late autumn of 1995 when I first came to be interviewed about the situation in the Prijedor area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you give a statement in late 1995 or autumn 1995 in connection with what you recollect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was interviewed. I don't know whether I gave a statement or not, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As far as you know, we went through it, Exhibit number 5 is the only statement that you recall giving in connection with your involvement in former Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you say so, yes. This, I remember giving this statement at a later date. That was on another case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's not if I say so, I just don't know. I'm asking you, if you think you have another statement, by all means tell us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think the witness has given evidence and Mr. Keegan has confirmed that there is one statement and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir -- if I may proceed? Sir, you testified about a book that you wrote, and is it fair to say that book was published in December, or thereabouts, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The book was completed in October 1993, it was out by the end of that year, formally published, I think, at the beginning of the following year, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the book that you wrote was professionally done, I mean, in terms of -- it was depicting your professional experiences and your views and things that you saw during your tenure in the former Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was written faster than I would like to have written it but, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It was part professional, part personal; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure what that means, but it was an account of what I had seen in the war, yes, and drew on a number of secondary sources which I have described to you. I researched books, documents, and other newspapers. Talked to colleagues a great deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know what "part personal and part professional" means either. I thought you used it when you said when you went to visit Dr. Kovacevic, that the reason you went to visit him was part personal and part professional?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I said that, fine. Yes. I was curious to find out --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: There is really no question pending, if I may? I just want to ask him that question, and the question is: What do you mean when you say "part personal and part professional"? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It means that if there was a story to write about this visit, to try to seek out these three gentlemen and Professor Koljevic, then I would write it, but I was also quite curious to know more about them. They had been introduced to me on a day that was important to me and I was curious.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: From 1994 -- when did you leave Bosnia completely? In December of 1994, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left Bosnia shortly after the conclusion of the siege of east Mostar, which would be February 1994, and I went to live in the United States for some months and I came back in the spring of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So is it fair to say from February 1994 through the spring of 1995, you were living in the United States; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was based in the United States but visiting Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's fair. Your part personal/part professional curiosity about Dr. Kovacevic and others in connection with the August 5th meeting that you had with them, during the time of July 19 -- or August 5th, 1992, through February 1995, right before you left the whole area, were you curious at all to meet him during that year-and-a-half period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left the area in February 1994, not '95.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was difficult for me to do so. I applied, along with many colleagues, to visit the -- it was then called the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and later on Republika Srpska a number of times, and like many of my colleagues was not allowed permission by the office of Sonja Karadzic who was handling press accreditation in Pale at the time. That was one reason it was difficult to get to Prijedor. I'm not the only one with that experience. And the other is that the preoccupation, as my statement shows, was with Muslim-Croat war in other parts of the country. I was not in a position or did not feel in a position to or was not allowed to travel to Prijedor until after the war had concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say for the period February 1994 through the spring of 1995, you did not have any desire or feelings to go to visit these people, including Dr. Kovacevic, back in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The war was still on then. I was living in the States, based in the States, and the occasion did not arise. I was working in America and also it -- I don't think I would have been allowed to go, frankly. I applied twice in Pale to visit and was not given clearance by Ms. Karadzic's press office.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, did your desire, if you will, to go back to meet Dr. Kovacevic and others, did that occur, part professional/part personal, before or after the meeting that you had with Mr. Keegan in Washington?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, after. It occurred as part of an assignment that I was given by The Guardian at the end of 1995. This was after the Dayton Agreement -- well, it was while it was being negotiated -- and the foreign editor of The Guardian said to me, "Well, you were in Bosnia all that time before. Why don't you go back and spend a number of months there and try and tell some of the untold stories of the war, try and get under the skin of the war a bit now that it is easier to move around?" That resulted in a twelve-part series, and after discussions with him, we decided that one dimension of this inquiry would be to go back and to find the people and to interview them with whom we had met in Prijedor that unforgettable day. That was the professional dimension. My personal curiosity that I mentioned accompanied that assignment. It was agreed as part of a series which is published and readily available.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you know, sir, following your first meeting with Mr. Keegan, that he wanted to utilise you as an expert?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew that there was a possibility that I would testify. I wasn't aware in exactly which capacity. I had had the interview here around the same time, a little prior, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so I understand, because there are two meetings with Mr. Keegan, and I need to just connect it up for a couple of reasons, and I apologise for belabouring the point. Your meeting with Mr. Keegan initially was in Washington, DC, the first one; the second one was here at The Hague; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did your desire to part personally and part professionally find Dr. Kovacevic, interview Dr. Kovacevic, in February of 1996, did that occur after the first or the second meeting with Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The assignment to write this series for the paper followed the second meeting with Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, isn't it true that during the second meeting with Mr. Keegan, it was during that meeting that, in fact, he inquired and asked you to establish this pattern and wanted you to become a witness, expert witness, in the Tadic or other related cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was clear that I was -- might testify, but I'm afraid I can't help you with the exact, you know -- I don't think we talked about what he wanted me -- I mean, he wasn't telling me what he wanted me to do or anything like that. He was interviewing me about the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I thought we covered it earlier. That's why -- I'm not as clear on it as I perhaps should be, and I'm sure you could help us out on that. You had two meetings with him. Earlier today you testified that at one meeting you were sought out and they requested your services to help them to become an expert witness to establish pattern; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I testified in the summer of 1996. By that time, certainly I was aware of this thing called "widespread or systematic." I don't know if I was aware of it when I first came here in 1995. I'm pretty sure I didn't know anything about these laws and rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In fact, you don't know anything about the laws, and I mean this respectfully, in connection with the elements, of the accused, et cetera; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. No, I don't want to say I don't know anything about the laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I appreciate --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have since read up as much as I can. But when I came to The Hague in the late autumn -- I can get the date for you easily -- for this first meeting, not in America with Mr. Keegan, I was pretty clueless as to Geneva Conventions and so on. I don't think I had read it then or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Keegan at all provide you materials so that you could become more familiar with what the Geneva Convention is or the laws in connection with the various trials that may be proceeding here at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did he explain to you at all what certain elements of crimes are, et cetera, at any time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe later on, towards the time I was testifying, but not at first, so far as I can recall. I was being interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just so we have it clear, because you've testified on two separate occasions, if not more, the time, was that the first time you testified in the Tadic case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time I testified before this Tribunal was in the case of Dusko Tadic in the summer of 1996. I don't recall the exact date. I think it was June or July.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In connection with the testimony that you're giving with Dr. Kovacevic, can you share with us what, if anything, you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In connection with the testimony that you're giving in this matter here, can you testify -- can you tell us what is it that you reviewed before you testified here a couple days ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I read my book, or read bits of it, and I read through some of the notes, but not in great detail, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you meet with anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met with Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: For how long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not very long. He's been very busy. I've been here since Saturday.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So with the exception of your notes, is it fair to say that you didn't review anything else in connection with the testimony that you were going to share with us here and are sharing with us currently relating to Dr. Kovacevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No -- yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I may, I'd like to direct your attention to August 5th, 1992, which is the first time that you met Dr. Kovacevic and the first time that you came to the Prijedor municipality building, okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who accompanied you during that first visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Major Milutinovic from Banja Luka, two film crews from ITN and their two translators, also two soldiers from the Bosnian Serb army who took us as far as Banja Luka, anyway, and a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to Major Milutinovic, was he dressed in a formal military garb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What did that look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Camouflage fatigues and a hat, sort of like a pork pie hat, we call them in English. I don't know what the respectful term is. Not a cap, a hat, with the insignia on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How long, sir, was the journey from Belgrade to Prijedor in terms of hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Belgrade to Prijedor? From Belgrade to Pale on the helicopter was, I don't know, an hour, hour and a half, maybe more; Pale to Banja Luka on the bus via a place called Bijeljina was the best part of a day, I wouldn't want to measure it in exact hours; Banja Luka to Prijedor, little time. Maybe 45 minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, the time we're talking about, Belgrade to Pale by helicopter, an hour and a half, Pale to Banja Luka, and Banja Luka to Prijedor, all occurred on August 5th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the witness has given evidence about that. It was a two-day journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I recognise that. I just wanted to point -- get a time reference on that and make sure that my notes are accurate that it was a two-day journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So it was actually August 4th; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me try to calculate this. I'll work backwards, if I may, if the Court will permit? August 5th, we're in the camps. So August 4th, we'd have been going from Pale to Banja Luka. The day before that, 3rd, we'd have travelled early to Pale and spent the day in Pale and in bits of Sarajevo, as discussed before.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Where did you spend the night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a hotel to which they took us, and I think it was near Pale somewhere. Somewhere near Sarajevo -- in what is now called Srpska Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So you had a fresh start the next day, August 5th, for your journey through Pale to Banja Luka to Prijedor; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The next day would have been August the 4th, and that would been, yes, an early start. From Pale, I think we had a snack in a place called Bijeljina, and then through the corridor to Banja Luka. That's the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Then you spent the night there and the next day you came on August 5th to Prijedor; correct? I'm trying to get there, and I apologise that it's taking long.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next day we got up in Banja Luka, and we went to Prijedor that morning, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What time did you arrive in Prijedor that morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember. Quite early on. I mean, it was quite an early start, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, yesterday you testified, I believe, that Dr. Kovacevic was the chairman and the person that controlled the meeting; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was sitting, as it were, at the head of the table, and did, well, I'd say most of the talking, but more than anybody else, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you recall your testimony yesterday in which you identified him as the "chairman" of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't mean that in a formal sense, but the meeting seemed to be -- he would speak when he wished to and -- I say "chairman," but he was running the meeting, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, in your opinion, that he was running the meeting and "he" being Dr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He? Yes, I said that Dr. Kovacevic appeared to be the man who opened the meeting and did most of the talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At any time, sir, did you say in any statements that were given that "Dr. Stakic chaired the meeting at the city hall before we went to the camp"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember writing that because I don't think he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I tender Defence Exhibit number 6? Again, I must apologise to the court and the Tribunal. We were unable to obtain the necessary copies because of a glitch in the photocopy machine there and there were other counsel attempting to copy, so it was quite mad. Tomorrow we hope to provide sufficient copies for everyone, and I apologise again. Thank you. May Defendant's Exhibit number 6 be tendered to the witness, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, can you describe what Defendant's Exhibit number 6 is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's my -- an aide-memoire I wrote after the interview with Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that was an interview that occurred in February of 1996; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Same day as seeing Dr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Isn't that a document which we already have?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I believe it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it's Exhibit 56, Prosecution Exhibit 56.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We already have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no need to exhibit it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The only reason I do, Your Honour, respectfully, is only because I wasn't sure if the exhibits in the closed session would carry on, and I wasn't sure if the procedure was I would have to introduce my own exhibits since we were in a closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've got the copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How would the Court like for me to refer to this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think, to ensure consistency, Exhibit 56, and D6 will be withdrawn. It will make life easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to Exhibit 56, can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just have. It's my notes written up in my organisation of the conversation with Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And your name appears on the top; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that the notes that you told us earlier that you actually made into your computer and placed on the disk and sent to Mr. Keegan, are those your notes -- or part of them, I should say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, do you see in that first paragraph on Exhibit number 56 that you make a reference to the meeting that you had on or about August 5th, 1992, with Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that if you look at that document, you, in fact, describe Dr. Stakic as the person who chaired the meeting on August 5th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was the senior titular official at the meeting and I suppose was formally in charge. What I was trying to say yesterday was that he didn't do most of the talking, he wasn't running the meeting. Indeed, at one point he tries to make a contribution and is told to shut up. But he was the senior official, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You say you suppose he was formally in charge. What do you mean by that, you suppose he was formally in charge? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the mayor, and I believe Dr. Kovacevic was his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the titles, sir. But who was in charge of the meeting on August 5th, 1992? You shared with us what you thought it was yesterday, and I'm asking you, in light of Exhibit 56, who, as you sit here now, who you thought it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the senior official was Dr. Stakic. The man doing the bulk of the talking was Dr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, show the Court where you reference him as "the senior man" on Exhibit 56.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You said that you felt that he was the senior official. Show me where you write "senior official" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I say "chaired the meeting."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So was it Dr. Stakic who chaired the meeting or was it Dr. Kovacevic who chaired the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll answer you like this: I'll say Dr. Stakic was the titular man in authority, he was the mayor, Dr. Kovacevic was his deputy and was doing the talking. He was the man who spoke when he wanted to. He sat in the middle at the head table.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, I think you did earlier -- and I'm doing it for a reason, Your Honour, so I'd like some latitude on it. Is it your testimony that Dr. Kovacevic was the man in control of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The main presence at the meeting, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me show what we're going to mark -- or has previously been marked, I believe, as Exhibit 55, and that is the statement that's typed regarding Dr. Kovacevic in the meeting in 1996. I just want to make sure that it's that number. I believe it is but ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Exhibit 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, can you describe for us what Exhibit 55 is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. These are notes that I made to myself into the computer, as previously discussed, in Zagreb the day, the evening after seeing the two gentlemen in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And those are the same notes as the Dr. Stakic notes that you tendered to Mr. Keegan; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you see a reference in the first paragraph there with respect to who was -- or who "assumed control" of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. Where are we?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On the fourth line down where it starts: Dr. Sakic (sic), and then it has a parenthesis, QV.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who does it say in that document was the person who "assumed control" of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He took over from Dr. Arsic when -- sorry, from Colonel Arsic where Colonel Arsic gestured to his right to say, "Well, if you want to go to Omarska, you have to speak to these gentlemen," and I think, as I testified yesterday, Mr. Stakic came next.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you see anywhere in Exhibit 55 whether or not you state that Dr. Kovacevic was the chair of the meeting on August 5th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't. I say that Mr. Stakic then passed our request on to Dr. Kovacevic for his handling.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you see on Exhibit number 55 anywhere that you state that Dr. Kovacevic was in control of the meeting on August 5th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, and I'm not saying "in control of," I'm saying doing most of the talking at, the main presence at.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so we're clear and I appreciate that. So he wasn't in control and he wasn't the chairman, he was doing most of the talking; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and when --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's all --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- the others wanted to interrupt him, he didn't let them --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We heard about that yesterday, and we hope to get to it again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine, do -- yeah, we will.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As you sit here, do you know who the main person was or who was the person who was in control or in charge of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've said this. Mr. Stakic was clearly the senior civilian official - he made a long presentation; Colonel Arsic was the main military man; and Dr. Kovacevic did most of the talking, sat in the middle; and between them, I don't say anyone had sole control of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you for sole control, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all talking. Mr. Kovacevic talked most.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, do you remember giving testimony in the Tadic case in 1996 in connection with particularly August 5th, 1992, and the meeting involving Dr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember it well, but I'm sure I'd have -- I'm sure I'd have mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may, on page -- if I may just have a moment to find the page? 1440, if I may direct the Court's and the Prosecutor's attention to it. Sir, do you recall giving -- may I proceed? I apologise. Do you recall giving the following testimony in connection with the meeting taking place on August 5th, 1995 -- 1992, thank you, I'm sorry, regarding Dr. Kovacevic, and I'm going to quote a question that begins on line 8, counsel, and then the answer on line 9 up to 13, unless the Court wishes us to read the prior page and the subsequent data. But for our purposes, I think it would be limited to this four-line or five-line area. Sir, do you remember being asked this question: "Did Dr. Milomir Stakic then enter into the discussion with you? Answer: Yes. Stakic came in briefly and made his main speech later on but, as it transpired, the people to whom we would appropriately apply to go to Omarska, who were in charge of Omarska ergo" -- strike that, Your Honour. I'm actually -- "who were in charge of Omarska ergo and the authority to take us there were indeed sitting in the room." Do you recall giving that testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I recall talking about it when I was testifying, but without -- I don't -- I mean, the exact words, frankly, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I want to direct the Court's attention to 1439 and not 1440, specifically line 10 through line 13. I was reading off my notes and looking at the page improperly. So if I can once again focus on this and look at page 1439, which specifically discusses who began the meeting and the issue that I'm trying to convey here. Thank you, Your Honour, and I apologise. 1439. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Line 10: "Who began the meeting for that group? Answer: The meeting was begun -- well, as it were, the pleasantries were begun by the police chief, Mr. Drljaca, but the main -- sort of the man who kicked off the meeting, as it were, was Colonel Arsic of the military." Do you remember giving that testimony, sir, in the Tadic case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember that actual line, but, yes. The pleasantries, or the introductory remarks as I called them yesterday, went, and I think this is right, in this order: Drljaca first downstairs when we arrived and on the stairs; then, as we saw yesterday, Kovacevic follows; Stakic I think then says something; and then we turn to the main body of the meeting, or at least the lengthy bits during which the conversations and the toeing and froing about Manjaca and Omarska and where we want to go and where we could go, where we couldn't go, that was with Colonel Arsic. So I'm going to call them the introductory remarks and/or pleasantries, then the main body of the meeting, if that's all right with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I have a moment, Your Honour? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, you said just now "yesterday, as we saw in the meeting." The tape that we saw yesterday, was that a tape that taped the beginning part of the meeting all the way through the end of the meeting of this August 5th, 1992 meeting with Dr. Kovacevic and others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did the meeting -- was the meeting taped at the very outset when the meeting started; is that when it started? The taping, the actual taping of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The film made by the ITN. That was towards the top of the meeting, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But it wasn't the beginning of the meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it wasn't the beginning, it was fairly close in to the beginning. I mean, it was within five or ten minutes of the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When's the first time that you viewed that tape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That particular tape?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That particular tape.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This weekend -- yesterday, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that for six years, you haven't viewed that particular tape; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw some stuff in Omarska and some stuff in Trnopolje when I was testifying in the Tadic case. I don't think I saw that bit of tape, no, at least I don't recall it anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your testimony is appearing here. It says: "If it wasn't the beginning, it was fairly close to in the beginning. I mean, it was within five or ten minutes of the beginning." Can you help me out and tell me whether it was five or ten minutes, or you just don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't within that kind of time frame, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So for that five- or ten-minute period, we don't have any tapes to see who started the meeting or what was said for that five- to ten-minute period; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what tapes you have or haven't got. My best recollection, and I'll do my best now, is that we were greeted downstairs by Mr. Drljaca and he escorted us up, and I think the others were already in the room. If not, they came in soon after. But as regards five to ten minutes, I'm afraid I can't help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the top of the meeting. It's what I've been calling the opening remarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I know, but it may be relevant for other reasons. Thank you. Sir, I'm a little confused now with respect to the August 5th, 1995. We've recognised that you identified various people as being, at one point, "chairman," "in control of," and I think perhaps stating this with Colonel Arsic being "the main, sort of, person." Who, in your opinion, having been an expert, do you think, based on all that data, do you think was in charge of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1992, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the meeting, yes, we're referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to sort of -- I will say no one was actually in charge of the whole thing, and I'll have to repeat myself, if the Court will allow me. Dr. Stakic was introduced to us as the senior official on the civilian side. He was, if you like, the formal chairman. Doing the running, the man to whom people referred at the end of their various contributions, was Dr. Kovacevic. If you want to ask me who was in sole command of the meeting, I'm afraid I have no real answer to that, and I would say none of them. They were all doing their own thing or looking after their own departments in their own way.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going to have any more questions on that topic. No doubt you're going to move on. In fact, it's 5.00. So we will adjourn. How much more do you have for this witness, do you think, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm very cognisant, we are very cognisant of the time element and the inconvenience this may bring to Mr. Vulliamy, and I say that very, very sincerely. However, a point, when we discussed the medical doctor, from our prior session and our notes confirmed one thing, and when I asked Mr. Vulliamy to read that particular portion with respect to the Muslim doctor in the Trnopolje camp, he read something slightly different. I haven't caucused with the balance of the Defence team, and I'm uncertain as to how complicated our notes and how possibly incorrect our notes might be until we've had an opportunity to review the entire transcript from this morning's session, and it may go on, unfortunately, longer than tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sure you will have the time constraints in mind, and if you can finish tomorrow, so much the better. If need be, no doubt we could sit a little longer than we intended.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll try my best, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
